title: Soupe au Pistou
subtitle: Provençal summer vegetable soup with basil pistou
excerpt: The summer soup of Provence: a clear, light broth of fresh vegetables and beans finished at the table with pistou, the French cousin of pesto, a rough paste of basil, garlic, and olive oil stirred in to fragrance each bowl.

recipe.sourceNotes: Soupe au pistou is the great summer soup of Provence and the Côte d'Azur, and a dish that shares its ancestry with Genovese minestrone al pesto: both regions face each other across the Ligurian Sea and share a culinary heritage of bean soups finished with pounded basil. Pistou (from the Provençal word for pound) differs from pesto in that it contains no pine nuts and traditionally no cheese (though parmesan is sometimes added); the result is lighter and more herbal. The soup uses whatever fresh summer vegetables are best at the market: courgettes, green beans, tomatoes, broad beans, new potatoes. The beans (white haricots or cannellini) provide body. The pistou is stirred in at the table, not cooked; heat destroys the fresh basil fragrance that is the whole point.

content.text: Make the pistou just before serving and do not cook it: the raw basil and garlic are the point. Stir each bowl at the table. The soup itself is forgiving; the pistou is not: use the best fresh basil and your best olive oil.

content.text: Heat 3 tablespoons of olive oil in a large pot. Cook the leek and carrot for 5 minutes. Add 2 litres of water, the potato, tomatoes, bay leaves, and thyme. Bring to a boil and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the courgette, green beans, and cannellini beans. Simmer for 10 minutes. Add the pasta and cook for the time stated on the packet. Season with salt. The soup should be lightly brothy, not thick.

Make the pistou: pound or blend the basil, garlic, and a pinch of salt to a rough paste. Stir in the olive oil. The texture should be coarse, not smooth. Serve the soup in wide bowls with a generous spoonful of pistou stirred in at the table.
